q: The piezoelectric effect is the production of:
o: ultrasound by heating a metal wire
light when electrons strike a screen
a potential difference across certain crystals when they are mechanically stressed
a magnetic field around a vibrating crystal
x: Crystals such as quartz develop a voltage when squeezed or stretched; the reverse effect (an alternating voltage makes the crystal vibrate) is used to send ultrasound, so one transducer both sends and receives.

q: An ultrasound pulse is reflected from a boundary inside the body and the echo returns 1 × 10⁻⁴ s after the pulse was sent. If the speed of ultrasound in tissue is 1500 m s⁻¹, how deep is the boundary?
x: The pulse goes there and back, so depth = vt/2 = 1500 × 10⁻⁴/2 = 0.075 m = 7.5 cm. Forgetting to halve gives 15 cm.

q: What is the wavelength of 3 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue where its speed is 1500 m s⁻¹?
x: λ = v/f = 1500/(3 × 10⁶) = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.5 mm. Treating MHz as 10⁵ instead of 10⁶ gives the tempting 5 mm.

q: Why is a gel spread on the skin before an ultrasound scan?
o: To cool the probe, which heats up while producing ultrasound
To increase the frequency of the ultrasound
To absorb the reflected echoes before they reach the probe
To remove air between the probe and the skin, so most of the ultrasound enters the body instead of being reflected
x: Air and skin differ greatly in acoustic properties, so an air gap reflects almost all the ultrasound at the surface. The gel removes the air and lets the pulse pass into the body and the echoes return.

q: In an ultrasound scan, echoes from the front and back surfaces of an organ return 40 μs and 60 μs after the pulse. If ultrasound travels at 1500 m s⁻¹ in the organ, what is its thickness?
x: The extra time is 60 − 40 = 20 μs for a round trip through the organ, so thickness = 1500 × 20 × 10⁻⁶/2 = 0.015 m = 1.5 cm. Forgetting to halve gives 3 cm; using 60 μs alone and halving gives 4.5 cm.

q: A CT (computed tomography) scanner forms its images by:
o: passing X-rays through the body from many angles and combining them by computer into cross-sectional slices
using strong magnetic fields and radio waves
detecting gamma rays from a positron-emitting tracer
x: CT rotates an X-ray source and detectors round the patient and a computer builds cross-sectional images. Strong magnets and radio waves describe MRI; gamma rays from a positron tracer describe PET.

q: On an ordinary X-ray image, bones appear lighter than the surrounding soft tissue because bone:
o: absorbs X-rays much more strongly than soft tissue
reflects X-rays back to the X-ray tube
lets X-rays pass more easily than soft tissue
x: Bone is denser and contains elements of higher atomic number (calcium), so it absorbs more X-rays; fewer reach the detector behind it, leaving that region light. Thinking bone transmits more is the reverse of the truth.

q: In PET scanning, what do the detectors around the patient actually record?
o: Positrons coming straight out of the body
X-rays passed through the body from an external tube
Pairs of gamma-ray photons moving in opposite directions, produced when positrons annihilate with electrons
x: The tracer emits positrons that travel only about a millimetre before annihilating with electrons, giving two gamma photons that move apart in opposite directions; detecting both at once locates the source line. The positrons themselves never leave the body.

q: An X-ray tube operates with an accelerating potential difference of 80 kV. What is the maximum energy of an X-ray photon it produces? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
x: The most energetic photon takes all of an electron's kinetic energy: E = eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 8 × 10⁴ = 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁴ J (80 keV). Using 80 V instead of 80 kV gives 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ J.

q: In PET, a positron and an electron, both practically at rest, annihilate into two gamma photons. What is the energy of each photon? (mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
x: Total energy = 2mₑc², shared equally by two photons, so each has mₑc² = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 9 × 10¹⁶ ≈ 8.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ J (0.51 MeV). Giving one photon the whole 2mₑc² gives 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.
